name: John Resig
milestone_by_age_26: Publicly released jQuery at BarCamp NYC in January 2006 at age 21; it became the most widely used JavaScript library.
early_history_summary: Resig studied computer science at Rochester Institute of Technology, conducting research on data mining and real-time collaboration and joining the Computer Science House. Frustrated by cross-browser JavaScript inconsistencies as a student, he began building jQuery in 2005 and unveiled it at BarCamp NYC in January 2006. The library was quickly adopted by Drupal and major companies, and he later authored Pro JavaScript Techniques (2006) while still a student.
primary_leverage_engine: Scarce technical depth in client-side JavaScript
primary_early_advantage_tags: RIT CS House, open-source community, Ajax/web platform wave, student project distribution
evidence_summary: Resig created jQuery as an RIT student in 2005–2006 and released it at BarCamp NYC at age 21, solving a scarce cross-browser DOM problem just as Ajax and rich web apps took off. Drupal and major tech firms adopted it rapidly; he later worked at Mozilla (2007–2011) and as chief software architect at Khan Academy. Family background is not documented in reviewed sources; early advantage appears primarily self-created technical depth plus open-source distribution rather than inherited capital or domain apprenticeship.
starting_point: Born in Boston, Massachusetts, in 1984; early family class and parental background not documented in reviewed sources; studied computer science at RIT.
current_position: Chief software architect at Khan Academy; creator of jQuery and ukiyo-e.org; lives in New York's Hudson Valley.

trajectory.event: Began developing jQuery while a student at RIT to address cross-browser JavaScript inconsistencies.
Publicly released jQuery at BarCamp NYC in January; later published Pro JavaScript Techniques.
Joined Mozilla Corporation as a JavaScript evangelist and tool developer.
Graduated RIT with a BS in computer science; jQuery won .Net Magazine Best Open Source Application award.
Joined Khan Academy, later becoming chief software architect and building its interactive CS curriculum.
Launched ukiyo-e.org, a large-scale Japanese woodblock print image-search archive for digital humanities.

name: Paul Sciarra
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Cold Brew Labs (with Ben Silbermann) was founded in 2008 (~age 27) and Pinterest launched around 2009–2010 (~age 28–29); birth year is only approximate (c. 1980–1981).
early_history_summary: Sciarra graduated from Yale University and worked at Radius Ventures before co-founding Cold Brew Labs with Ben Silbermann in 2008, which incubated Pinterest. He served as Pinterest's early president/CEO, left in 2012, then became an entrepreneur-in-residence at Andreessen Horowitz and later executive chairman of Joby Aviation.
evidence_summary: Reliable sources place Sciarra's birth around 1980–1981 and Yale graduation in the early 2000s. The co-founding of Cold Brew Labs (2008) and Pinterest (~2010) both fall after age 26 on that birth-year range. No earlier material, dated founding or product milestone by 26 was verified.

name: Tom DeMarco
milestone_by_age_26: No material personal milestone by age 26 found. Joined Bell Labs in 1963 (~age 23) on ESS-1 as employment; defining work on structured analysis (Structured Analysis and System Specification, 1978–79) and Peopleware came in his late 30s and later.
early_history_summary: DeMarco earned a BSEE from Cornell, an MS from Columbia, and a diplôme from the University of Paris. He started at Bell Labs in 1963 on the ESS-1 electronic switching system, then worked in European IT consulting on conveyor and online banking systems before becoming a leading figure in structured analysis in the 1970s.
evidence_summary: Born 1940 in Hazleton, Pennsylvania. Early Bell Labs employment on ESS-1 is a strong start but not a personal breakthrough product, paper, or founding. Field-defining publications and Atlantic Systems Guild work arrived well after age 26.

name: Bruce Artwick
milestone_by_age_26: Founded Sublogic in October 1977 at age 24 after a 1976 master's thesis demonstrating real-time computer-generated flight display; released the first consumer Flight Simulator for Apple II around 1979–early 1980 (age 26–27).
early_history_summary: Artwick grew up in Norridge, Illinois, attended Triton Junior College, then studied electrical engineering at the University of Illinois (BS 1975, MS 1976), working in the Digital Computer Lab and Aviation Research Lab and becoming a pilot. His May 1976 thesis showed real-time flight display on microprocessors; he founded Sublogic in 1977 and shipped A2-FS1 Flight Simulator for Apple II, later licensed to Microsoft as Microsoft Flight Simulator (1982).
primary_leverage_engine: Scarce technical depth in real-time 3D graphics / simulation
family_context_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources beyond growing up in Norridge, Illinois.
primary_early_advantage_tags: UIUC Digital Computer Lab, Aviation Research Lab, pilot training, personal computing wave, Stu Moment partnership
evidence_summary: Artwick combined UIUC lab access, pilot training, and a 1976 thesis on dynamic flight display into Sublogic (1977, age 24) and the first consumer flight simulator (~1979–80). University facilities and domain immersion were catalytic; family background is undocumented. Microsoft licensed the product in 1982; he later founded BAO Ltd., which Microsoft acquired in 1995.
starting_point: Born January 1, 1953, and raised in Norridge, Illinois; family class/parental occupations not documented; path ran through Triton Junior College into UIUC electrical engineering.
current_position: Creator of the Flight Simulator franchise lineage; Sublogic and BAO founder; living; Microsoft acquired BAO and Flight Simulator rights in 1995.

trajectory.event: Completed UIUC master's thesis demonstrating a versatile computer-generated dynamic flight display on microprocessors.
Founded Sublogic to commercialize microcomputer flight simulation software.
Released A2-FS1 Flight Simulator for Apple II (and TRS-80), the first major consumer flight simulator.
Microsoft licensed the product and released Microsoft Flight Simulator for the IBM PC.
Left Sublogic and founded the Bruce Artwick Organization (BAO) to continue Flight Simulator development.
Microsoft acquired BAO and the Flight Simulator copyright; Artwick continued as a consultant.

name: Ginni Rometty
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Joined IBM as a systems engineer in 1981 at age 24 (standard early career hire); became IBM's first female CEO in 2012 at age 54.
early_history_summary: Born Virginia Nicosia in Chicago in 1957; her father left when she was young and her mother raised four children with limited means. She joined IBM in 1981 after college and spent decades rising through technical, consulting, and leadership roles before becoming CEO (2012–2020).
family_context_summary: Raised in Chicago; father left when she was young; mother raised four children with limited formal education and resources.
parent_family_domain_summary: No parental tech or executive domain advantage documented.
evidence_summary: Rometty's defining public milestone was becoming IBM CEO in 2012, decades after age 26. The 1981 IBM systems-engineer hire is ordinary entry-level employment, not a material personal breakthrough by the project's standard.

name: Vincent Aleven
milestone_by_age_26: No confirmed birth year found; cannot verify age at milestones. Co-founded Carnegie Learning in 1998 after a 1997 Pitt PhD; TU Delft studies (1980–1988) suggest mid-career timing for major work, but age ≤26 cannot be established.
early_history_summary: Aleven earned an MS in computer science from TU Delft (1988) and a PhD in Intelligent Systems from the University of Pittsburgh (1997), then joined Carnegie Mellon as a postdoc. He co-founded Carnegie Learning and researches intelligent tutoring systems and CTAT at CMU HCII.
evidence_summary: Without a documented birth year, age at Carnegie Learning founding (1998) or earlier milestones cannot be verified against the ≤26 rule.

name: Edward Yang
milestone_by_age_26: No confirmed birth year found; cannot verify age ≤26. MIT BS 2012 and Stanford PhD 2017 with FAIR/PyTorch work from ~2017; if a typical college-age cohort, major PyTorch contributions likely at or after ~26–27.
early_history_summary: Edward Z. Yang (ezyang) earned a BS in computer science from MIT (class of 2012) and a PhD from Stanford (2017), then joined Facebook AI Research as a research engineer working on PyTorch internals and ML systems.
evidence_summary: No public birth year for Edward Z. Yang. Defining professional role on PyTorch at Meta begins around PhD completion in 2017; without birth year, age-26 eligibility cannot be established.

name: Hal Finney
milestone_by_age_26: No career-defining material milestone by age 26 found. After Caltech he programmed Intellivision/Atari games at APh (from ~1978, age 22) as employment; PGP work, RPOW (2004), and first Bitcoin transaction (2009) all came well after age 26.
early_history_summary: Born in Coalinga, California, in 1956 to a petroleum engineer father; graduated Arcadia High School (1974) and Caltech EE (1979). Worked at APh Technological Consulting on Intellivision and Atari games through the mid-1980s, later became second developer hired for PGP, created RPOW, and received the first Bitcoin transaction from Satoshi Nakamoto in 2009. Died of ALS in 2014.
family_context_summary: Father Harold Thomas Finney was a petroleum engineer; family later lived in Arcadia, California.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father in petroleum engineering; no documented crypto or computer-science domain transfer.
evidence_summary: Early APh game programming (Space Battle, Star Strike, etc.) was solid commercial work by his mid-20s but not the field-defining breakthrough for which he is known. Cypherpunk activism, PGP, RPOW, and Bitcoin all date from his 30s–50s.

name: Lennart Augustsson
milestone_by_age_26: No confirmed birth year found; cannot verify age at Lazy ML / HBC milestones. Co-developed Lazy ML and published a compiler paper in 1984; later built HBC (early Haskell compiler), but age ≤26 cannot be established.
early_history_summary: Swedish computer scientist associated with Chalmers University of Technology; co-developed Lazy ML with Thomas Johnsson in the early 1980s, authored an LML compiler paper (1984), created the HBC Haskell compiler, and later worked at Facebook, Google, and Epic Games on languages including Verse.
evidence_summary: Important FP language work is well documented from the mid-1980s onward, but without a birth year age-26 eligibility cannot be verified.

name: Adrian Cockcroft
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Born 1960; programmed as a teen and worked at Sun from the mid-1980s, but defining books (Sun Performance and Tuning) and Netflix cloud architecture leadership came in his 30s–40s (Netflix from 2007, ~age 47).
early_history_summary: British engineer who programmed as a child in the early 1970s, joined Sun Microsystems (UK then US), authored Sun Performance and Tuning, later worked at eBay Research Labs, led Netflix cloud architecture (~2007–2013), and held senior roles at Battery Ventures and AWS.
evidence_summary: Self-reported birth year 1960 in interview; early programming interest is noted but no dated, material personal product/founding/award by 1986 (age 26). Fame rests on Sun performance books and Netflix cloud migration much later.

name: Boris Schaling
milestone_by_age_26: No confirmed birth year found; cannot verify age at any milestone. Known for The Boost C++ Libraries (first edition ~2011); no dated material achievement by age 26 can be established.
early_history_summary: Boris Schäling (often Anglicized Schaling) is the author of The Boost C++ Libraries, a widely referenced introduction to Boost with hundreds of examples, published in multiple editions from around 2011 onward.
evidence_summary: Book publication around 2011 is the main public milestone; without a birth year, age-26 eligibility cannot be assessed.
